title: A decision that changes life
summary: Baptism is a public confession of faith and an identification with the death and resurrection of Jesus - believer's baptism by immersion. We speak gently about "rebaptism" after a childhood baptism, emphasizing that it is a declaration of readiness, not haste, and that the strength to persevere comes from Jesus himself. This closes the series and is an invitation to the daily decision to walk with God.

sections.heading: Baptism: a public confession and new life

items.comment: Baptism is an identification with the death and resurrection of Jesus: going under the water pictures the burial of the old life, and coming up out of it - rising to a new life. It is not just a ceremony, but a passage from the old life into the new.

questions.text: What in your "old life" would you want to be "buried," and what would you want to be born anew?

items.label: baptism as being buried and raised with Christ (Rom 6:3-4)
items.content: In Rom 6 baptism is an image of three movements: going under = being buried with Christ in his death, coming up = being raised with him to a new life, and the whole = a real inclusion in his story of salvation. Baptism does not "add" merit, but publicly expresses what grace has already done. New life and obedience are the fruit of this union with Christ, not a condition of salvation - grace comes first.

questions.text: How does understanding baptism as "being buried and raised with Christ" protect against treating it as a work by which one "earns" something?

items.comment: In sending out the disciples, Jesus joins baptizing with teaching. Baptism is part of the normal path of following Jesus - a step he himself invites us to, not an add-on for the "very religious."

questions.text: How does the fact that baptism is a direct command of Jesus affect the way you think about it?

items.label: baptism "in the name" of the Trinity (Matt 28:19)
items.content: Jesus commands us to baptize "in the name (singular) of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit." The singular "name" alongside three Persons is one of the biblical foundations for belief in the Trinity. The Greek *eis to onoma* ("into the name / into the ownership of the name") was also a formula for the transfer of ownership: the baptized person is "signed over" as the possession of God - Father, Son, and Spirit. So baptism is a public entry into relationship with the whole Godhead.

questions.text: What does it mean that in baptism you are "signed over as the possession" of the Father, Son, and Spirit - rather than merely taking part in a rite?

items.comment: When his listeners ask what they should do, Peter joins the call to repentance with baptism. Baptism is therefore a response to conversion - the outward expression of an inward decision.

questions.text: How does baptism as an "expression of the heart's decision" differ from baptism treated as a mere ritual?

items.comment: Paul describes baptism as clothing oneself with Christ. It is the public "putting on" of a new identity - from now on I belong to him.

questions.text: What would it mean for you to "clothe yourself with Christ" before others, and not only in your heart?

items.label: "clothe yourself with Christ" (endyo) (Gal 3:27)
items.content: The Greek *endyo* means "to put on, to clothe oneself" - like a garment. The baptized have "clothed themselves with Christ" as with a robe of new identity. In antiquity, a change of garment signified a change of status (for example, a slave who became free). The image says: in baptism I take off the "old clothing" of my former life and put on Christ - from now on he is my identity, visible to others.

items.comment: Jesus himself was baptized, and the description of him coming up out of the water points to immersion. His baptism is the pattern: conscious, voluntary, by immersion, confirmed by the presence of the Father and the Spirit.

questions.text: What does it say to you that Jesus himself, though sinless, chose baptism as an act of obedience and identification with us?

items.comment: The Ethiopian first believes, and then both go down into the water and come up out of it - the account clearly implies immersion preceded by a confession of faith. First faith, then baptism.

questions.text: Why does the order in this story - first understanding and faith, then baptism - matter?

items.comment: Here too Jesus comes up out of the water - another image of baptism by immersion, not sprinkling. The very biblical term (Greek *baptizo*) means "to immerse."

questions.text: How does the symbolism of immersion (burial-and-rising) capture the meaning of baptism better than sprinkling alone?

items.label: "to baptize" means "to immerse" (baptizo)
items.content: The Greek *baptizo* means "to immerse, to plunge" (from *bapto* - "to dip"), also used of dyeing fabric by immersing it in dye. The very term implies immersion in water, not sprinkling. This fits with the descriptions of coming up out of the water (Matt 3:16; Mark 1:10; Acts 8:39) and with the symbolism of burial and rising (Rom 6:3-4) - which sprinkling can hardly convey.

items.comment: Paul presents baptism as being buried with Christ and raised together with him - accomplished through faith. This is why baptism implies the conscious decision of a believing person.

questions.text: What does it mean that baptism is effective "through faith," and not in and of itself, as a rite?

items.comment: The text links receiving baptism with believing the gospel that was preached. The biblical pattern is baptism preceded by personal faith and decision - something an infant cannot yet make. We speak about this gently and without judging anyone.

questions.text: If biblical baptism implies personal faith, how can you look calmly at a baptism received in infancy, without one's own decision?

items.comment: The disciples who had earlier received John's baptism, after a fuller understanding, receive a baptism that now points them directly to the Lord Jesus. A conscious identification with Christ after a mature decision is not a lack of respect for the earlier experience - it is a response to new understanding.

questions.text: Is a baptism of conscious faith after a childhood baptism a "rebaptism," or rather a first conscious step of faith? What does this text suggest?

items.label: "rebaptism" and infant baptism (Acts 19:1-5)
items.content: In Acts 19:1-5 the disciples at Ephesus, earlier baptized with John's baptism, after a fuller knowledge of the gospel receive a baptism that points them to the Lord Jesus. The text shows that a conscious baptism after an earlier, incomplete experience is not a slight to that experience, but a response to new understanding. In the case of a baptism received in infancy (without personal faith and decision), a conscious believer's baptism is therefore not a "repetition" of the same thing, but a first personal confession. We speak about this gently, without judging individuals or families - the measure remains the biblical pattern: faith, then baptism (Mark 16:16; Acts 8:12). The critique concerns the practice and the teaching, never people.

questions.text: Why, according to the biblical pattern (faith, then baptism), can a conscious baptism after an infant baptism be understood as a "first step of one's own," rather than a repetition?

items.comment: The call to receive baptism is addressed to the adult Paul, who has just consciously turned to God. Baptism here is a personal, conscious act of response to grace.

questions.text: What would it mean to hear such a call to baptism as addressed personally to you?

sections.heading: A declaration of readiness, not haste

items.comment: Jesus uses the image of a builder who first counts the cost. Baptism is a declaration of readiness to walk with God, a conscious decision - not a rash gesture of "straight to the baptistery."

questions.text: What would it mean for you to "count the cost" before deciding to follow Jesus?

items.label: "counting the cost": a decision, not an impulse (Luke 14:28)
items.content: Just before the image of the builder who "counts the cost," and the king weighing whether to go to war, Jesus speaks of carrying the cross and following him. He does not discourage the decision - on the contrary, he wants it to be conscious and lasting, not a fleeting surge of emotion. This is the biblical basis for the practice that baptism is preceded by preparation and understanding. The paradox of grace: salvation is free, but following Jesus encompasses a whole life - which is why it is worth entering it with open eyes.

questions.text: How does a "counted" decision (conscious, lasting) differ from a decision made only under the emotion of the moment?

items.comment: Joshua calls the people to choose this very day whom they will serve. Faith is a conscious choice - and baptism is its public confirmation. No one makes it for us.

questions.text: If faith is a choice, at what stage of that choice are you today?

items.comment: Jesus is presented as the one who stands at the door and knocks - he invites, but does not force it open. The decision to go further is yours; baptism is the conscious opening of that door.

questions.text: What is "knocking" in you today as you think about your next step with God - and are you ready to open?

sections.heading: The strength to persevere comes from Jesus

items.comment: In the image of the vine and the branches, Jesus shows that without him we can do nothing. Walking with God does not rest on the strength of our own will, but on remaining in him. He is the one who gives the strength to persevere.

questions.text: What does it mean in practice to "remain" in Jesus day by day, so as to draw strength from him and not from yourself?

items.comment: Paul expresses confidence that God, who began a good work in believers, will himself bring it to completion. This work is his responsibility - which lifts the pressure of "managing on your own."

questions.text: How does it change your approach to perseverance to know that God has committed himself to complete his work in you?

items.label: "one baptism" and the community of the journey (Eph 4:5)
items.content: Paul names "one Lord, one faith, one baptism" (Eph 4:5). Baptism is therefore not a private experience, but an entry into a community that has one Lord and one faith. So you do not take your next step alone: you become part of a family that walks together after the same Jesus. Perseverance is easier in community - and that is God's design (compare Heb 10:24-25).

items.comment: Right after the words about baptism, Jesus promises his constant presence to the end of time. So you take your next step not alone - he goes with you.

questions.text: What does the promise of Jesus' constant presence - not only his company at the start - mean for your decision?

items.comment: Paul confesses that he can do all things through the one who strengthens him. Perseverance does not depend on your reserves, but on the power of Christ - available afresh every day.

questions.text: In the face of what concrete "I can't do it" would you want to lean today on the strength of Jesus rather than your own?

application.text: This is the last step of this series - and the first step of the rest of the journey. Baptism is not a formality or a reward for the "perfect": it is a public confession that you belong to Jesus, and an identification with his death and resurrection - the old life buried, the new one begun. The biblical pattern is believer's baptism by immersion, preceded by a personal decision; this is why a conscious baptism after a childhood baptism is not a lack of respect, but your first "yes." It is not about the haste of "straight to the baptistery," but about a sincere declaration of readiness. And the strength to persevere is not something you have to summon from within yourself - it is given by the one who promised to be with you always and to complete the work he began in you.
application.challenge: Answer one question honestly before God: "Am I ready to consciously follow Jesus and express it in baptism?" If yes - take a step of declaration: talk with someone in God's family about preparing for baptism. If not yet - tell Jesus plainly what is holding you back, and ask him to give you the readiness and the strength (John 15:5; Phil 1:6).
